findings.title: No null-check on integration.metadata['sender']
findings.body: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] assumes the integration metadata always contains a 'sender' key. build_integration only sets metadata['sender'] if state.get('sender') is truthy, so integrations created without that state field will raise KeyError here instead of failing gracefully with the intended error() response. This can turn an auth-mismatch case into an unhandled 500.

findings.title: safe_urlopen response not checked for errors before reading
findings.body: req = safe_urlopen(...) is used without verifying the HTTP status code succeeded. If GitHub returns a non-200/error response (e.g., invalid client credentials), the code still attempts safe_urlread/parse_qsl which may not raise, silently falling into the generic 'access_token not in payload' error path, but earlier failures (5xx, connection reset) are only caught by the broad except Exception around parsing, which could mask legitimate operational issues instead of surfacing a clearer failure mode in logs.

findings.title: Overly broad bare except swallows parsing errors silently
findings.body: The except Exception: payload = {} catches all exceptions from safe_urlread/parse_qsl without logging, making it hard to diagnose failures (e.g., network errors, decode errors) in production. At minimum this should log the exception for observability.

findings.title: installation_id from query bound to pipeline state without validation
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, installation_id from request.GET is bound directly to pipeline state before any OAuth validation occurs. Since this happens prior to verifying state/signature or exchanging the code, an attacker could manipulate the installation_id value on the initial request if it influences later authorization flow, since the binding happens unconditionally on every dispatch call (including the first redirect leg).

findings.title: Changed error message not clearly justified by test name
findings.body: test_installation_not_found now expects 'Invalid installation request.' instead of the previous specific 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' message. This generic message change reduces the clarity of error feedback to users when the installation lookup fails for unrelated reasons (e.g., state mismatch here), and the test doesn't verify that build_integration's IntegrationError path is actually exercised anymore -- the failure in this test is actually due to signature mismatch, not the installation-not-found code path, so the test name is now misleading.
